title: Digestive and Urinary Systems

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the structure and function of the digestive tract and its accessory organs.
- Describe the structure and function of the urinary system, including the nephron and the process of urine formation.
- Recognize common digestive and urinary conditions and apply the medical office assistant's role in accurate documentation, patient communication, and escalation.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of the GI tract as a long water slide: food enters at the mouth, slides down the esophagus tube into the stomach pool, then winds through the long small intestine and the wider large intestine before it exits.

### Question 2

Imagine a kitchen: the GI tract is the conveyor belt the food rides on, and the liver, gallbladder, and pancreas are the helpers standing beside it adding their special juices to the food.

### Question 3

Mechanical digestion is like tearing a big sheet of paper into tiny scraps with your hands; chemical digestion is like the scraps then dissolving in water.

### Question 4

Chemical digestion is like a key unlocking a padlock: special worker molecules called enzymes open up the big food pieces into tiny building blocks the body can use.

### Question 5

Peristalsis works like squeezing a tube of toothpaste from the bottom up: each squeeze pushes the contents a little farther along.

### Question 6

Your spit already has a helper enzyme that starts dissolving starchy foods like bread the moment you chew it, a little like a cleaner that starts working on contact.

### Question 7

The esophagus is the delivery slide that carries each bite from your throat down into your stomach.

### Question 8

The lower esophageal sphincter is like a one-way door at the top of the stomach that should only open when food arrives from above.

### Question 9

The stomach is like a blender that turns your bite of food into a thin, soupy smoothie called chyme before sending it to the next station.

### Question 10

Your stomach is the first protein-chomping station: its acid and a worker enzyme called pepsin start snipping the long protein strings into shorter pieces.

### Question 11

The small intestine is the main loading dock where the tiny nutrient building blocks get moved into the blood so the body can use them.

### Question 12

Villi are like the thick shag of a carpet: all those tiny fingers add lots of surface so more nutrients can be grabbed at once.

### Question 13

The small intestine has three neighborhoods in a row: Duo-Jej-Ile — like three train cars named Duodenum, Jejunum, and Ileum, in that order.

### Question 14

The large intestine is like the drying room at the end of the line: it soaks up leftover water and packs what's left into a solid form the body can pass.

### Question 15

The liver is the factory that makes bile, and the gallbladder is the little storage tank next door that keeps it until it's needed.

### Question 16

The gallbladder is the body's bile storage locker: it saves the liver's bile and squirts it out just when a fatty meal shows up.

### Question 17

Bile works like dish soap on greasy water: it breaks one big oil blob into lots of tiny droplets so the fat-digesting enzymes can reach more of it.

### Question 18

The pancreas is a two-job helper: it squirts digestive scissors and an acid-neutralizer into the small intestine, and it also makes hormones like insulin for the blood.

### Question 19

The pancreas wears two hats: one hat squirts digestive helpers into the gut, and the other hat drips sugar-controlling hormones into the blood.

### Question 20

If peristalsis is a conveyor belt moving food forward, segmentation is a gentle squeezer that kneads and mixes the food with the digestive juices right where it is.

### Question 21

Fats take a special side door out of the intestine — a little lymphatic tube called a lacteal — while sugars and proteins hop straight into the blood.

### Question 22

Defecation is the final 'out' step of digestion — the body's way of taking out the trash after the food's useful parts have been collected.

### Question 23

The gallbladder is a storage closet, not a chef — it holds the bile the liver made but doesn't cook up any enzyme helpers of its own.

### Question 24

Digestion is a four-step relay race: take the food in, break it down, collect the good stuff, and throw away the leftovers — in that exact order.

### Question 25

The small intestine is like a folded towel: if you spread out all its folds and tiny finger-like bumps, it has a huge area for soaking up nutrients.

### Question 26

The stomach wears a raincoat of slippery mucus on the inside so its own strong acid doesn't burn a hole in it — like wearing gloves before handling something harsh.

### Question 27

The urinary system is a four-part cleanup crew: two kidney filters, two drain tubes (ureters), one storage bag (bladder), and one exit tube (urethra).

### Question 28

Each kidney is packed with about a million tiny filter units called nephrons — like having a million mini water-purifiers working side by side.

### Question 29

The kidneys are the body's water-filter plant: they clean the blood, keep the right amount of water and salts, and send the trash out as urine.

### Question 30

The glomerulus is like a fine mesh strainer inside the kidney: blood pressure pushes the liquid and tiny particles through the mesh, leaving the big blood cells behind.

### Question 31

Reabsorption is the kidney's 'keep' pile: as the filtered liquid flows by, the kidney grabs back the water and sugar the body still needs.

### Question 32

Secretion is the kidney's 'last chance' to throw extra trash into the urine — like a final sweep of leftover litter into the bin after the main sorting.

### Question 33

The ureters are the two drain pipes that run from the kidney filters down to the bladder storage tank.

### Question 34

The bladder is the holding tank that waits until it's full, then lets you know it's time to go to the bathroom.

### Question 35

The urethra is the final exit pipe that lets urine leave the body; the ureters are the earlier pipes that bring urine down to the bladder.

### Question 36

A shorter exit tube means germs outside the body don't have to travel as far to reach the bladder — like a shorter hallway to a room.

### Question 37

Urine is like a river: it starts at the kidney spring, flows down the ureter channel into the bladder lake, and pours out through the urethra outlet.

### Question 38

The kidneys are more than filters — they also send a chemical message called erythropoietin to the bone marrow telling it to make more red blood cells.

### Question 39

When the kidneys sense blood pressure dropping, they ring a chemical alarm bell called renin that helps the body push blood pressure back up.

### Question 40

ADH is the body's water-saver switch: when you're low on water, it tells the kidneys to hold onto more instead of flushing it out.

### Question 41

Urine is mostly just water with a little dissolved trash mixed in — like the water you use to wash your hands, carrying away the dirt.

### Question 42

When the body recycles old proteins, the leftover nitrogen gets bundled into a waste called urea, which the kidneys flush out in urine.

### Question 43

The bladder has a two-gate exit: one gate closes on its own, and the other gate is one you can control, which is why you can usually 'hold it.'

### Question 44

Arteries deliver, veins drain: the renal artery brings dirty blood into the filter, and the renal vein carries the cleaned blood back out.

### Question 45

The collecting duct is the final mixing station where the kidney decides how much water to keep, making the urine stronger or weaker.

### Question 46

The kidneys are the body's salt-and-water managers, carefully adjusting the recipe of the blood so it stays just right.

### Question 47

The detrusor is the bladder's squeeze muscle — when it's time to go, it tightens like a hand squeezing a water balloon.

### Question 48

The kidneys are the body's water treatment plant, and a treatment plant needs a big, steady river of water flowing through it all day to keep things clean.

### Question 49

The kidneys help 'switch on' vitamin D so the body can soak up the calcium it needs for strong bones.

### Question 50

The kidney's filter is like a screen with very small holes: water and tiny salts slip through, but big proteins and blood cells are too big and stay behind.

### Question 51

GERD happens when the stomach's top door doesn't shut all the way, so acid splashes back up the food pipe and stings it.

### Question 52

A tiny germ called H. pylori can set up camp in the stomach and wear a sore into its lining — like a splinter that keeps irritating the same spot.

### Question 53

Gastritis is a stomach-ache word: 'gastr' means stomach and '-itis' means it's swollen and angry, like a scraped knee on the inside.

### Question 54

Pain that travels to the lower right belly can be the appendix acting up, and the appendix is like a little finger that can burst — so it's a 'get help right now' situation.

### Question 55

Gallstones are little rocks that form in the gallbladder's storage tank when the bile gets too concentrated — like sugar crystals forming in syrup.

### Question 56

When you eat a fatty meal, the gallbladder squeezes out bile; if stones are blocking it, that squeeze hurts — like squeezing a tube with a plug in it.

### Question 57

Cholecystitis is the gallbladder's own 'angry' condition — the word for gallbladder (cholecyst) with the '-itis' ending for swelling.

### Question 58

Hepatitis is the liver's 'angry' word — 'hepat' means liver and '-itis' means swollen, so the liver is inflamed.

### Question 59

Cirrhosis is when the liver gets covered in scar tissue — like a sponge that has been scratched and hardened so it can't soak things up anymore.

### Question 60

Diverticula are like tiny balloon pockets that form on the colon wall; when those pockets get irritated or infected, that's diverticulitis.

### Question 61

IBS is like a fussy gut that acts up with cramps and bathroom changes even though tests don't show a broken part.

### Question 62

Think of Crohn's as spots of trouble that can pop up anywhere along the food pipe, while ulcerative colitis is one long patch of trouble that stays in the colon.

### Question 63

In celiac disease, a protein called gluten makes the body attack the little finger-like villi in the gut, flattening them so fewer nutrients get soaked up.

### Question 64

If waste sits in the colon too long, the colon keeps squeezing water out of it until it dries into hard little lumps that are hard to pass.

### Question 65

When the colon rushes stool through too fast, it doesn't have time to soak up the extra water, so the result is runny and loose.

### Question 66

Hemorrhoids are puffy, swollen veins around the bottom — like varicose veins, but in the area where stool leaves the body.

### Question 67

If blood travels a long way through the gut, it gets digested into a black, tarry mess (melena); if it's fresh and bright red (hematochezia), it came from closer to the exit.

### Question 68

A colonoscopy is a tiny camera on a tube that takes a tour through the colon to look for polyps before they can become cancer.

### Question 69

A bladder infection usually announces itself with burning when you pee, needing to go often, and a sudden 'I have to go NOW' feeling.

### Question 70

Pyelonephritis is when the infection climbs all the way up to the kidney, bringing fever and a sore spot in the back where the kidney lives.

### Question 71

A kidney stone is a tiny rock passing through the urinary pipes, and as it scrapes along it causes sudden, very strong side pain and sometimes blood in the pee.

### Question 72

CKD is when the kidney filters slowly wear out over years, like a water filter that gradually gets clogged and can't be swapped out.

### Question 73

Acute kidney injury is a sudden 'stall' of the kidney filters over a short time, while chronic disease is a slow fade over years.

### Question 74

Glomerulonephritis is when the kidney's tiny filter units get swollen and leaky — so things that should stay in the blood, like protein, slip out into the urine.

### Question 75

Incontinence is when pee leaks out without the person meaning to let it go — the body's 'gate' isn't holding like it should.

### Question 76

The prostate sits like a doughnut around the urine exit pipe; when it gets bigger, it squeezes the pipe and makes peeing slow and difficult.

### Question 77

Blood in the pee is like a warning light on the dashboard — you don't ignore it; you tell the person who knows how to check under the hood.

### Question 78

Black, tarry stool can mean blood is being digested inside the gut — a sign to get help quickly, not to wait it out.

### Question 79

When a lot of water leaves the body through diarrhea, the body can dry out like a plant without water, which is especially risky for older people — so it's time to call for help.

### Question 80

A clean-catch is like letting the first bit of water flush the dust out of the spout, then catching the clean middle stream in the cup.

### Question 81

Collecting a stool sample is like catching a food sample for testing: keep it clean, keep it separate from other liquids, and deliver it fresh.

### Question 82

The assistant's job is like a relay runner: listen to the symptom, write it down, and pass it along to the doctor or nurse — never decide it's no big deal.

### Question 83

Melena is the medical word for the black, tarry stool that can mean blood has been digested on its way through — a sign the doctor needs to know about.

### Question 84

Pain under the right ribs after a greasy meal is a big clue pointing to the gallbladder, the little bile tank that squeezes when you eat fat.

### Question 85

Fever with a sore spot over one kidney is the body's alarm that an infection may have reached the kidney — a reason to get medical help right away.
